analysis.one_liner: Ends federal tax credits for wind and solar power after 2030 and denies clean energy credits to foreign adversary-linked companies.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by a Republican with 10 Republican cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee since its May 2025 referral with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end the federal clean electricity tax credits for wind and solar facilities that begin construction after 2030, while leaving the same credits in place for other power sources like nuclear, geothermal, and hydrogen. It would also bar companies controlled by the governments of China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea from claiming a long list of federal clean energy tax breaks. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Producers of power sources that would keep their tax credits while wind and solar lose theirs, such as nuclear, geothermal, hydrogen, and natural gas, would face less subsidized competition. The federal treasury would save the cost of the wind and solar credits that end. Companies with no ownership ties to the four named countries would face a cleaner competitive field under the foreign-entity ban.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes wind and solar facilities from eligibility for the clean electricity production and investment tax credits when construction begins after December 31, 2030, while leaving the credits available for other technologies.

It prohibits entities created or controlled by the governments of China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea, or controlled by such entities, from claiming a broad list of federal clean energy tax credits, including credits for nuclear, hydrogen, carbon capture, clean vehicles, and advanced manufacturing.
Supporters argue wind and solar are mature technologies that no longer need federal support, and that blocking adversary-linked firms from energy tax breaks addresses a national security concern.

analysis.who_pays: Wind and solar projects that start construction after 2030 would lose tax credits worth a substantial share of project cost, which developers would likely recover through higher electricity prices or by building less. The public would bear higher power costs and a slower buildout of the cheapest new generation sources; the foreign-entity restriction would deny credits to any US-based projects backed by capital from the four named countries.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wind and solar developers; electricity customers

drawbacks.text: Ending wind and solar credits while keeping them for nuclear, hydrogen, and other sources raises the cost of building the technologies that currently supply much of the cheapest new electricity, a cost that would likely show up in household power bills.

The foreign-entity prohibition is broad: it reaches any entity 'controlled' by even one company tied to a listed government, which could sweep in domestic projects with minority foreign backing and chill investment.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the savings come at the cost of less clean generation capacity, and that the credits already phase down under current law, so the additional deficit savings are modest relative to the effect on power supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The national security restriction on adversary-linked firms is the part with the clearest broad benefit and little public downside. The core of the bill, ending wind and solar credits on a delayed timeline while preserving credits for competing technologies, costs a specific industry billions and risks higher electricity prices for households, with the offsetting benefit of some federal savings. On balance the bill's main effect favors some energy producers over others, not the public over an industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Jennifer Kiggans introduced the bill in the House on May 8, 2025, joined by Reps. Garbarino, Valadao, Newhouse, and Amodei as original cosponsors.
Ten Republicans had signed on as cosponsors when the bill was referred.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Ways and Means on May 8, 2025, and the full action history shows no further steps, hearings, markups, or votes.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet and nothing has changed: because the bill never advanced, the existing wind and solar tax credits remain in place, so wind and solar developers are better off than they would have been under the bill, and electricity customers face no new cost from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wind and solar developers, so far

for.name: Rep. Jennifer Kiggans
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 10 cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Garbarino, Valadao, Newhouse, and Amodei

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat has signed on; no vote has occurred, so the full partisan split is not yet known.

industries.industry: Wind and solar developers and equipment makers
industries.note: The bill strips wind and solar facilities out of the clean electricity tax credits for projects starting after 2030, removing support worth a large share of project cost. Because these are among the cheapest sources of new power, the industry's loss in this bill runs alongside a likely cost to household electricity bills.

industries.industry: Nuclear, geothermal, hydrogen, and gas-fired power producers
industries.note: The bill keeps the same clean electricity credits available to non-wind/solar facilities, so competing power sources would face less subsidized competition. Households could pay more for electricity as a result, though some of these technologies also lower emissions.

industries.industry: Companies tied to the governments of China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea
industries.note: Any entity created or controlled by these governments would be barred from a long list of energy tax credits, including credits for clean vehicles, nuclear, hydrogen, and carbon capture. Their loss is the intended national security gain for the public.

industries.industry: US clean energy manufacturers and project developers generally
industries.note: The foreign-entity ban cuts off one source of foreign capital for US clean energy projects, which defenders call a security necessity and developers may experience as a loss of investment. The wind and solar sunset hits the sector directly, while credits for other technologies survive.

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this rarely get standalone floor votes; major tax-code changes in this Congress are expected to move through the budget reconciliation process, where majority control can pass them without minority support. The wind and solar credit rollback is already the subject of broader tax legislation, so this bill's most likely fate is to sit in committee as a statement of position unless its provisions are folded into a larger package.
